references.text: Jacob bought the birthright from Esau, which shows that the birthright could be transferred, but the Mosaic law here forbids a father from arbitrarily changing the natural order of inheritance based on feelings toward his wives.
Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and Leah became the 'hated' wife. This situation with one beloved wife and one less-loved wife is directly parallel to the context in Deuteronomy 21.
Jacob blessed Ephraim over Manasseh, the firstborn. This shows a case where the birthright was changed, but this happened through prophetic guidance, not because of favoritism toward a wife.
Reuben lost his birthright because of his sin, not because of his father's favoritism toward another wife.
The birthright was given to Joseph's sons because Reuben defiled his father's bed. This shows that the birthright could be removed due to serious sin, but not through arbitrary favoritism.

Rehoboam loved Maacah more than all his other wives and made her son Abijah leader among his brothers, even though he was not the firstborn. This can be seen as a violation of the principle in Deuteronomy 21:16.
